name: Overconfidence effect
statement: Overconfidence names three separate errors, and the verdict below is about one of them, excessive certainty, which holds in the field but not across the ways researchers elicit it.
meaning: Moore and Healy split the word into three claims that had been run together. Overestimation is thinking one's own score, ability or chance of success is higher than it is. Overplacement is thinking one stands higher than other people than one does. Overprecision is holding a belief with more certainty than the evidence supports, which shows up as confidence intervals that are too narrow. The three are measured by different tasks and can be present at once in opposite directions. Someone can be sure they failed an exam, be wrong about that, and still have been far too sure. An entry that treats the three as one effect is describing something no study has measured.

origin.who: Don A. Moore and Paul J. Healy
origin.note: The split is a reorganisation of a literature that was already three decades old. Moore and Healy searched PsycINFO for "overconfidence" and got 365 hits, 72% of them empirical. Roughly 64% of the empirical studies measured overestimation, roughly 31% measured overprecision and roughly 5% measured overplacement. A search on "better-than-average" returned another 146 articles, so that last figure understates how much the comparison had been studied under a different name. The calibration tradition they were tidying runs back to Lichtenstein, Fischhoff and Phillips's 1982 review and to Alpert and Raiffa's interval task in the same volume.

evidence: Moore and Healy put 82 Carnegie Mellon students through 18 trivia quizzes of ten items each, three quizzes on each of six topics, one easy, one medium and one hard. Pay was $25 times a participant's percentile rank, belief reports were scored by a quadratic rule, and earnings averaged $20.23 for about 90 minutes. Beliefs were elicited three times per round: before the quiz, after taking it, and after the answers were shown. The figures below are the interim ones, taken after the quiz and before feedback, which is how the paper's two results tables are labelled. Actual scores were 8.86 on easy quizzes, 5.92 on medium and 0.71 on hard. Estimated scores moved much less, at 8.64, 5.93 and 1.50. Participants therefore underestimated themselves on easy quizzes by 0.22 points and overestimated on hard ones by 0.79, which Moore and Healy identify as the hard-easy effect on estimation. Overplacement ran the other way, at plus 0.48 on easy quizzes and minus 1.36 on hard. Across the 18 quizzes the two measures correlated at r(18) = -.64, p = .004. Overprecision alone pointed one way throughout. Intervals representing 90.5% confidence held the true score 73.1% of the time, a rate pooled across the three phases and produced by none of them separately, since hit rates ran 55.1% before the quiz, 85.6% after it and 84.4% after feedback. Confidence exceeded accuracy at every difficulty, every round and every phase. Eighteen rounds of full feedback did not teach participants to make fewer errors estimating their scores.

replication.headline: The verdict is about overprecision, which survives at scale in the field and does not survive a change of elicitation, while overestimation and overplacement reverse direction with task difficulty.
replication.detail: Ben-David, Graham and Harvey collected 13,346 one-year probability distributions for S&P 500 returns from senior finance executives, most of them chief financial officers, across quarterly surveys from June 2001 to March 2011. Realised returns fell inside the executives' 80% confidence intervals 36.3% of the time, and 59% of the time even in the least volatile quarters of the sample. The average interval was 14.5% wide, against a 42.2% gap between the 10th and 90th percentiles of realised one-year returns, and 3.4% of executives gave an interval wider than 42.2%. Boutros, Ben-David, Graham, Harvey and Payne extended that panel to over 28,400 forecasts and report no improvement with task repetition and no learning in response to past performance, which their abstract reads as miscalibration being a persistent personal trait. Moore, Tenney and Haran report that overprecision generalises across cultures, genders, professions, ages, levels of expertise and elicitation formats, and that the known moderators shrink it without removing it. The other two components hold up less well. Juslin, Winman and Olsson's review of the two-alternative general knowledge literature reports very little support for a cognitive-processing bias and near elimination of the hard-easy effect once scale-end effects and linear dependency are controlled, which the hard-easy effect entry, no. 247, sets out at length. Overprecision has a matching problem one level down. Li, Hale and Moore ran 402 people through three unrelated tasks, forecasting baseball games, Raven's matrices and guessing weights from photographs, and analysed 381. Inter-task correlations averaged 0.12 for overestimation, 0.10 for overplacement and 0.68 for overprecision, though on that measure their sample was underprecise rather than overprecise. In a later study they recruited 326 people, analysed 242, and asked each how sure they were of a single estimate in four ways: a Likert scale, an incentivised bet, a 90% interval and a probability distribution. Those four agreed at an average of r = .11, against .46 in the authors' simulation of an agent holding one coherent distribution.

study.cite: Ben-David, I., Graham, J. R., & Harvey, C. R. (2013). Managerial miscalibration. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 128(4), 1547-1584.

limits: The 90% confidence interval, the standard tool for overprecision, is not incentive-compatible. Moore, Tenney and Haran make the point plainly: paying for hit rates buys infinitely wide intervals, paying for narrowness buys the opposite, and balancing the two depends on beliefs the researcher cannot see. They also report that the width of a 90% interval bears a weak relationship to other measures of confidence, and that investors' trading volume is predicted better by the belief that one is better than others than by interval width. Prims and Moore found the direction of the result turning on the elicitation, and call it embarrassing how poorly different measures of overprecision correlate with one another. Their participants' estimated variance exceeded the actual variance, which is underprecision, while the same people were on average 46% sure they had named their own score exactly and were right 18% of the time, t(183) = 14.29, p < .001. Brenner's reply to Erev, Wallsten and Budescu argues that splitting observed confidence into true and artefactual parts gives precedence to a theoretical construct over the data. Erev, Wallsten and Budescu's own 1994 paper is closed at the publisher, with no repository copy listed by OpenAlex and none found at CiteSeerX or Academia, so what it showed is taken here from Brenner's abstract and from Merkle, Sieck and Van Zandt, who describe it as showing that the relation between confidence and proportion correct changes according to which of the two is computed as a function of the other. Alpert and Raiffa's founding numbers, 98% intervals holding the answer about 60% of the time and interquartile ranges holding it about a third of the time, are quoted here from Moore, Tenney and Haran's chapter. The original chapter was searched for again on this pass at Cambridge Core, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and the Internet Archive, and no copy was reachable, so the figures stand at one remove. Moore and Healy's own sample was 82 students answering general knowledge questions, recruited by a posting headed Tons o' Trivia on a site that recruits experimental participants. The authors note that this was likely to attract trivia enthusiasts.
misreadings: The line about drivers rating themselves above average is an overplacement result and belongs to illusory superiority, entry no. 47, which carries the better-than-average material. It says nothing about whether anybody is too certain. The reversal on hard tasks belongs to the worse-than-average effect, no. 266. Running the three components together is the error Moore and Healy set out to correct, and their own data show two of them moving in opposite directions across the same 18 quizzes. Whether overconfidence is a property of a person is open and being fought over in print. Li, Hale and Moore report mixed evidence for trait-like consistency and firmer evidence that overconfidence varies with situation and context. Binnendyk, Li, Costello, Hale, Moore and Pennycook then ran a preregistered adversarial collaboration on 942 American adults, using tasks whose outcomes are effectively random so that ability cannot drive the correlations, and their abstract reports robust relationships across tasks and supports the trait reading. Three of those authors appear on both papers. The familiar classroom finding that stated confidence beats accuracy on general knowledge questions measures two things at once, because being too sure of a binary answer is overestimation and overprecision together.
